answers.answer: No. De minimis releases associated with good faith attempts to recycle or recover refrigerants are not subject to the venting prohibition when an applicable compliance route is satisfied. Good faith alone does not suffice: except for exempt substitutes, releases qualify as de minimis only if they occur when either (i) the applicable practices in §§ 82.155 and 82.156, the applicable practices in § 82.157 (for appliances with class I or class II refrigerants or blends), required recovery/recycling machines under § 82.158, technician certification rules in § 82.161, and reclamation requirements in § 82.164 are observed, or (ii) the requirements in subpart B of 40 CFR part 82 are observed.

answers.answer: No. The de minimis exception does not excuse those requirements; rather, under paragraph (a)(2)(i), observing applicable servicing practices and using qualifying recovery/recycling equipment are affirmative conditions required for non-exempt releases to qualify as de minimis. Moreover, paragraph (b) independently prohibits maintaining, servicing, repairing, or disposing of an appliance containing a class I, class II, or non-exempt substitute refrigerant without observing the practices in §§ 82.155, 82.156, and 82.157 and using equipment certified under § 82.158.

answers.answer: No. The venting prohibition contains a separate exemption for specific substitutes in specific end-uses that exempts them both from the prohibition and from the requirements of the subpart. Examples include carbon dioxide, nitrogen, and water in any application, as well as specified uses of ammonia, chlorine, hydrocarbons, ethane, propane, isobutane, and R-441A.
